data.name: Title
data.value: A broad principal can read LAPS password attributes

data.name: EncryptedRead
data.value: This attribute stores an encrypted LAPS password. Read permission allows retrieval of the encrypted value, if present; it does not by itself grant permission to decrypt it. This finding does not establish that this principal can obtain the local administrator password or take control of the machine.

data.name: ClearTextRead
data.value: This attribute stores a LAPS password in clear text. If a password value is present, reading it exposes the local administrator password and may enable local administrative access.

data.name: EveryAttributeReach
data.value: The entry carries no object type, so it reaches every attribute on this object rather than only this LAPS attribute - which is the blanket extended-rights grant Microsoft warns about, because all LAPS password attributes are confidential.

data.name: WhyItMatters
data.value: A broad principal has read access to a LAPS password attribute. A clear-text value can expose the local administrator password; an encrypted value requires separate decryption permission. Read access alone is not proof of password retrieval or control of the machine. The principal is usually not the one named in the permission: it falls out of the group nesting underneath it, which is why nobody notices. Microsoft describes finding delegations that, expanded, reveal thousands of accounts holding local administrator rights.

data.name: WhatToDo
data.value: Follow the membership path on the finding and cut the link that brings the broad principal into the delegated group, or narrow the permission so it names only the administrators who need it. Do not simply remove the delegation: this product cannot know which principals your organisation intended to hold LAPS read access, and the group named may be entirely legitimate apart from what is nested inside it. Where the permission carries no object type it reaches every attribute on the object rather than only this LAPS attribute, and Microsoft's Find-LapsADExtendedRights cmdlet is the way to review that on an organizational unit.

data.name: About
data.value: Reports a computer whose LAPS password attributes can be read by a principal that is broad in every organisation, found by expanding whichever principal the permission actually names all the way down. It reports only that, and deliberately: nothing in the directory says which principals an organisation intended to hold this access, so a rule firing on an 'unexpected' principal would be imposing somebody else's idea of normal. The scope a permission is inherited from is stated as a fact rather than as an error, because a delegation made high in the tree may be deliberate. Every LAPS password attribute is confidential, which Microsoft says requires both Read Property and Control Access to read - this rule requires both before reporting anyone, so it names fewer principals than a tool testing Control Access alone, and every one it names has permission to read the attribute. For encrypted values, decryption permission is separate and is not established by this rule. A Control Access grant on its own is recorded as a fact and is not reported as an exposure. Disabled computer accounts are out of scope, having no running machine behind them, and a forest whose schema carries no LAPS attribute is not reported at all. Where the membership walk could not reach everything nested inside a delegated principal, the finding says so rather than implying nothing else is inside.
